summary.text: Assuming only finitely many such primes, let \(M\) be their maximum and apply the positivity hypothesis at \(n=M+3+2M^2\); the resulting decomposition \(n=p+q\) has \((\phi(p)\phi(q))^4+1\le M\), hence \(p\le M+1\) and \(\phi(q)\le M\). The prime-factor formula for the totient gives the general bound \(q\le 2\phi(q)^2\), so \(q\le2M^2\) and therefore \(n\le M+1+2M^2\), contradicting the choice of \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function. For each natural number \(n\), let
\[
a(n)=\#\left\{p<n: p\text{ is prime and }
 \bigl(\varphi(p)\varphi(n-p)\bigr)^4+1\text{ is prime}\right\}.
\]
Because \(p<n\), putting \(q=n-p\) always gives \(q>0\) and \(n=p+q\). We assume that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>2,
\]
and prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\).

We first establish the elementary estimate
\[
 m\le 2\varphi(m)^2 \tag{1}
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). This estimate is the ingredient that will allow us to bound an integer in terms of its totient.

Let \(S\) be the finite set of distinct prime divisors of \(m\), let \(k=|S|\), and put
\[
 P=\prod_{r\in S}r,
 \qquad
 R=\prod_{r\in S}(r-1).
\]
The usual prime-factor formula for the totient gives
\[
 \varphi(m)=\frac{m}{P}R. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(m=\prod_{r\in S}r^{e_r}\), then
\(\varphi(m)=\prod_{r\in S}r^{e_r-1}(r-1)\), which is exactly (2). Since \(m>0\) and \(P\mid m\), the integer \(m/P\) is at least \(1\). Consequently, (2) also gives
\[
 R\le \varphi(m). \tag{3}
\]

Every prime \(r\) satisfies \(r\ge2\), and hence
\[
 r\le 2(r-1).
\]
Multiplying this inequality over all \(r\in S\) yields
\[
 P\le 2^kR.
\]
As \(m=(m/P)P\), multiplication by \(m/P\), followed by use of (2), gives
\[
 m\le \varphi(m)2^k. \tag{4}
\]

We next compare \(2^k\) with \(R\). If \(2\notin S\), then every \(r\in S\) is at least \(3\), so every factor \(r-1\) is at least \(2\). Thus
\[
 2^k\le R.
\]
If \(2\in S\), remove \(2\) from \(S\). The factor contributed by \(2\) to \(R\) is \(2-1=1\), while each of the remaining \(k-1\) factors is at least \(2\). Therefore
\[
 2^{k-1}\le R,

after which multiplication by \(2\) gives \(2^k\le2R\). In either case we have the uniform bound
\[
 2^k\le2R. \tag{5}
\]
Combining (4), (5), and (3), we obtain
\[
 m\le\varphi(m)2^k
   \le 2\varphi(m)R
   \le 2\varphi(m)^2,
\]
which proves (1).

We now prove the desired infinitude by contradiction. Suppose that the set
\[
 \mathcal P=\{\ell\in\mathbb N:\ell\text{ is prime and }
              \ell=x^4+1\text{ for some }x\in\mathbb N\}
\]
is finite. Since it is a finite set of natural numbers, it has a common upper bound; choose \(M\) so that
\[
 \ell\le M\qquad\text{for every }\ell\in\mathcal P. \tag{6}
\]
(For instance, one may take the maximum of \(\mathcal P\), with \(0\) as a harmless convention if the set is empty.) Define
\[
 C=2M^2
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 N=M+3+C.
\]
Plainly \(N>2\). By the assumed positivity of \(a(N)\), at least one integer \(p<N\) satisfies
\[
 p\text{ is prime},
 \qquad
 \bigl(\varphi(p)\varphi(N-p)\bigr)^4+1\text{ is prime}. \tag{7}
\]
Put
\[
 q=N-p.
\]
Because \(p<N\), we have \(q>0\), and of course
\[
 N=p+q. \tag{8}
\]
Finally, set
\[
 x=\varphi(p)\varphi(q).
\]
The second assertion in (7) says that \(x^4+1\) is prime. It is therefore an element of \(\mathcal P\), and (6) gives
\[
 x^4+1\le M. \tag{9}
\]
For every natural number \(x\), one has \(x\le x^4\): this is immediate for \(x=0\), while for \(x\ge1\) it follows by multiplying \(x\) by three further factors each at least \(1\). Hence (9) implies
\[
 x\le M. \tag{10}
\]

We now derive separate bounds for \(p\) and \(q\). Since \(p\) is prime,
\[
 \varphi(p)=p-1>0. \tag{11}
\]
Also, since \(q>0\), its totient is positive:
\[
 \varphi(q)>0. \tag{12}
\]
Because both factors in \(x=\varphi(p)\varphi(q)\) are positive integers, each factor is at most their product. Thus, using (10),
\[
 \varphi(p)\le x\le M,
 \qquad
 \varphi(q)\le x\le M. \tag{13}
\]
From (11) and the first inequality in (13),
\[
 p-1\le M,

and therefore
\[
 p\le M+1. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(q>0\), estimate (1) applies to \(q\). Together with the second inequality in (13), it gives
\[
 q\le2\varphi(q)^2\le2M^2=C. \tag{15}
\]
Using (8), (14), and (15), we conclude that
\[
 N=p+q\le (M+1)+C. \tag{16}
\]
But by its definition,
\[
 N=M+3+C,
\]
which is strictly larger than \(M+1+C\). This contradicts (16).

The supposition that \(\mathcal P\) is finite is therefore impossible. Hence there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\), as claimed.
